verdict.label: apparent_contradiction
verdict.rationale: Both abstracts report an irisin–glucose correlation, but with opposite signs: A reports a negative correlation (r = -0.259, p = 0.039) in adults undergoing cholecystectomy or bariatric surgery in Brazil, while B reports a significant positive correlation (p < 0.001) in adolescents/young adults with PCOS and controls. The abstracts support a concrete contextual difference: A is a prospective cohort of predominantly adult surgical patients (mean age 46 ± 14 years) with plasma irisin, whereas B is a cross-sectional study of adolescents and young adults with PCOS using fasting serum irisin. PCOS is defined by insulin resistance and previous studies reported elevated circulating irisin in adult females with PCOS, and B's population shows markedly higher irisin levels (17.07–22.06 ng/ml) than A's groups (9.1–10.7 ng/ml). This population and disease-context difference (PCOS/insulin resistance vs. surgical obesity cohorts) could explain the opposite correlation directions.

source_evidence.quote: Irisin was negatively correlated with weight (r = -0.246; p = 0.042), waist circumference (r = -0.272; p = 0.024), glucose (r = -0.259; p = 0.039), glycated hemoglobin (r = -0.283; p = 0.024), triglycerides (r = -0.414; p = 0.024), and positively correlated with HDL (r = 0.280; p = 0.029).
The study subjects were predominantly female (75%), white (82%), with a mean age of 46 ± 14 years.
The findings revealed a significant positive correlation of serum irisin levels with BMI, glucose, insulin, HOMA-IR, LH, estradiol, and testosterone(all p-values < 0.001).
Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is a prevalent hormonal condition defined by insulin resistance.

Lean cases of PCOS had significantly elevated levels of fasting serum irisin (PCOS = 17.07 ± 5.61 ng/ml vs lean controls = 11.04 ± 7.51 ng/ml; p = 0.002), glucose, insulin, homeostasis model of assessment-insulin resistance index (HOMA-IR), luteinizing hormone (LH), estradiol, and testosterone and significantly lower levels of quantitative insulin sensitivity check index (QUICKI) compared to the lean controls.

diagnostics.notes: Extraction fields verified against sources: A's negative direction (r = -0.259) and B's positive direction (p < 0.001) both match their abstracts. Same exposure (circulating irisin) and same outcome (glucose) with comparable association-type contrasts. Opposite directions with a text-supported population/disease-context difference (PCOS adolescents/young adults vs. adult surgical cohorts; serum vs. plasma sampling) supporting apparent_contradiction with factor other.
